name: Victor Wembanyama
notes: A 7'4" French phenom whose final Metropolitans 92 season (21.6/10.4/3.1 blk, youngest-ever Pro A MVP, leading the league in scoring, rebounds and blocks) drew comparisons to no prior prospect — LeBron James called him "more like an alien." San Antonio took him 1st, the first French No. 1 pick. Wembanyama won unanimous Rookie of the Year and became the first rookie ever on the All-Defensive First Team, then developed into a genuine generational two-way superstar — 2026 unanimous Defensive Player of the Year (youngest ever), All-NBA First Team, Western Conference Finals MVP, and a 26/11.2 Finals run in a five-game loss to New York — despite a scary deep vein thrombosis diagnosis that shut down his 2025 season. Hit: the generational, unicorn-level outcome projected, arriving on schedule.

name: Brandon Miller
notes: Alabama's SEC Player of the Year and consensus Second-Team All-American as a freshman (18.8/8.2/2.1, an Alabama freshman record 41-point game, SEC Tournament MVP), elite pure scoring on a winning No. 1-seed team, though an infamously poor NCAA Tournament shooting stretch raised late doubts. Charlotte took him 2nd. Miller delivered immediately (17.3 ppg, All-Rookie First Team) and kept climbing (21.0, then 20.2 ppg) before wrist surgery in 2025 and shoulder surgery in 2026 interrupted otherwise clear star-level growth (19.0 career). Hit: elite college scoring that became a genuine, high-volume NBA star scorer, health the recurring question.

name: Scoot Henderson
notes: A G League Ignite prodigy who signed pro at 17 (the youngest in G League history, 15.6/5.7 over two seasons, exhibition matchups against Wembanyama), electric athleticism and playmaking as one of the most hyped prep prospects in years. Portland took him 3rd. Henderson's transition proved bumpier than expected (14.0, then 12.7 ppg on modest efficiency) and a hamstring tear cost him time in 2025-26, though a 31-point playoff game (youngest Trail Blazer ever with 30+ in a playoff game) showed real star flashes. Mixed outcome: real athletic point-guard talent still finding NBA-level efficiency and health.

name: Amen Thompson
notes: An Overtime Elite product (bypassing college with twin brother Ausar) and All-OTE First Teamer (16.4/5.9/5.9), elite explosive athleticism and playmaking on an unconventional development path. Houston took him 4th, one spot ahead of his brother — the first twins ever top-5 in the same draft. Ankle injuries slowed his rookie year, but Thompson developed into a genuine two-way force — a first career triple-double, All-Rookie honors, then All-Defensive First Team in 2025 — signing a $208M extension in 2026. Hit: real, elite non-college athleticism that became a genuine All-Defensive-caliber NBA star.

name: Ausar Thompson
notes: Amen's identical twin, an Overtime Elite two-time Finals MVP and 2022-23 OTE MVP (16.3/7.1/6.1/2.4 stl), elite defensive versatility from the same unconventional path. Detroit took him 5th, one pick after Amen. A promising rookie year (8.8/6.4) was cut short by blood-clot treatment in March 2024, but Thompson returned to lead the NBA in steals and earn All-Defensive First Team honors in 2025-26, finishing third in Defensive Player of the Year voting. Hit: real defensive-versatility upside that became a genuine, healthy-again All-Defensive NBA player.

name: Anthony Black
notes: A five-star Arkansas freshman (12.8/5.1/3.9/2.1 stl, a 22 ppg Maui Invitational stretch, SEC All-Freshman), real size-and-playmaking versatility at guard from a thin one-year sample. Orlando took him 6th. Black needed two patient development years (4.6, then 9.4 ppg) before a real 2025-26 breakout — 15.0/3.8/3.7 with a career-high 38-point game — while appearing in the playoffs every season. Hit: patient, multi-year development that produced a genuine, ascending NBA guard.

name: Bilal Coulibaly
notes: A French developmental prospect who broke into Metropolitans 92's senior roster alongside Victor Wembanyama (21.9/2.6 stl/1.2 blk with the U-21 squad), real long-term two-way upside on a thin professional sample. Indiana took him 7th (traded to Washington for Jarace Walker's rights). Coulibaly started immediately (the youngest Wizard ever to start a game) and grew steadily (8.4 to 12.3 to 11.7 ppg) through a wrist fracture, a hamstring strain and thumb surgery, and won a 2024 Olympic silver medal with France. Hit: real long-term two-way upside developing into a genuine young NBA starter, despite a run of injuries.

name: Jarace Walker
notes: A five-star IMG Academy recruit and Houston's AAC Rookie of the Year (11.2/6.8/1.8, Second-Team All-AAC), real positionless size and defense from a winning program. Washington took him 8th (traded to Indiana for the rights to Coulibaly). Walker needed two patient years behind Pascal Siakam and Obi Toppin (3.6, then 6.1 ppg) before a real 2025-26 breakout (11.6/5.1/2.5 across 41 starts) — an ankle injury cost him Indiana's 2025 NBA Finals appearance after their Eastern Conference Finals run. Solid outcome: patient positional development into a genuine, valuable NBA rotation piece.

name: Taylor Hendricks
notes: UCF's highest-ranked recruit ever and a program-record nine-time AAC Rookie of the Week winner (15.1/7.0, All-AAC Second Team), real modern stretch-four upside from a one-and-done season. Utah took him 9th, UCF's first lottery pick. Hendricks's rookie year showed promise (7.3/4.6) before a fractured fibula and dislocated ankle wiped out his entire 2024-25 season; he returned in 2025-26 with real flashes (back-to-back 20-point games) before a February 2026 trade (part of the Jaren Jackson Jr. deal) sent him to Memphis. Mixed outcome: real shooting-big upside repeatedly interrupted by a serious leg injury.

name: Cason Wallace
notes: A five-star Kentucky freshman and Texas Player of the Year in high school (11.7/4.3/3.7/2.0 stl on 44.6/34.6% shooting), elite two-way guard feel. Dallas took him 10th (traded to Oklahoma City for the rights to Dereck Lively II). Wallace won All-Rookie Second Team honors immediately (6.8/1.5), then developed into a genuine two-way piece on OKC's 2025 championship team (returning from a shoulder injury for the playoffs) before an All-Defensive Second Team selection in 2025-26. Hit: elite two-way college guard play that became a real NBA rotation piece and champion.

name: Jett Howard
notes: Michigan's leading three-point maker as a freshman (14.2 ppg, a 34-point game, All-Big Ten Third Team, son of coach Juwan Howard), real shot-making pedigree from a lottery-adjacent recruit. Orlando took him 11th. Howard's rookie chance stayed minimal (1.6 ppg) and his role has grown only marginally since (4.5, then 5.5 ppg with improving three-point shooting) before a 2026 two-way signing with Dallas. Bust: real shooting pedigree that thin opportunity has kept from becoming consistent NBA production.

name: Dereck Lively II
notes: A five-star Duke freshman and Morgan Wootten National Player of the Year in high school, elite shot-blocking on a limited offensive role (5.2/5.4/2.4 blk, ACC All-Freshman and Defensive teams). Oklahoma City took him 12th (traded to Dallas). Lively started immediately and helped Dallas reach the 2024 Finals as a rookie (8.8/6.9/1.4, All-Rookie Second Team), continuing solid production (8.7/7.5/1.6) before an ankle stress fracture and season-ending foot surgery in 2024-25, then further limited 2025-26 action. Mixed outcome: a real, valuable Finals-run starting center, health the recurring interruption.

name: Gradey Dick
notes: Kansas's Second-Team All-Big 12 freshman (14.1/5.1/1.7 on 44.2/40.3% shooting, Gatorade National Player of the Year in high school), elite shooting pedigree. Toronto took him 13th. Dick's rookie role stayed limited (8.5 ppg) before a real 2024-25 breakout (14.4 ppg, all starts, a 32-point game) — a right knee injury then ended his 2025-26 season early after a slower start (6.0 ppg). Mixed outcome: a real, if injury-interrupted, developing NBA shooting guard.

name: Jordan Hawkins
notes: UConn's First-Team All-Big East sophomore and 2023 national champion (16.2/3.8/1.3 on 40.9/38.8% shooting, West Regional Most Outstanding Player, 16 points in the title game), elite shooting from a champion. New Orleans took him 14th. Hawkins's production grew from 7.8 to a real 10.8 ppg role in 2024-25 before shrinking back to 5.1 ppg in a reduced 2025-26 role. Mixed outcome: real shooting talent that has yet to hold a consistently expanding NBA role.

name: Kobe Bufkin
notes: A McDonald's All-American whose Michigan sophomore breakout (14.0/4.5/2.9, Third-Team All-Big Ten, a 28-point game) suggested real guard upside. Atlanta took him 15th. Bufkin's career has been repeatedly interrupted by injury — a fractured thumb, a toe sprain, season-ending shoulder surgery — with real G League scoring flashes (23.6, then 25.2 ppg) never translating to a sustained NBA role across Atlanta, Brooklyn and the Lakers; he signed with New Orleans after a strong 2026 Summer League. Bust: real guard talent that injuries have repeatedly kept from an NBA opportunity.

name: Keyonte George
notes: Baylor's Big 12 Freshman of the Year (15.3 ppg, the second-most points in program history, a program-record 20 games of 20+ points), elite scoring volume on shaky efficiency (37.6/33.8%). Utah took him 16th. George won All-Rookie Second Team honors (13.0 ppg) and grew every season — 16.8, then a 2025-26 breakout to a career-high 23.6 ppg on markedly improved shooting (45.6/37.1%), including a 43-point game. Hit: real, high-volume scoring talent that steadily improved into a genuine go-to NBA scorer.

name: Jalen Hood-Schifino
notes: Indiana's Big Ten Freshman of the Year (13.5/4.1/3.7, a program freshman-record 35-point game, the highest-rated Hoosier recruit in years), real scoring and playmaking upside on a one-year sample. LA Lakers took him 17th. A lumbar microdiscectomy limited his rookie chance severely (1.6, then 2.0 ppg over 23 total games) before a 2025 trade to Utah (part of the Luka Dončić deal) and an immediate waiver; a Philadelphia two-way deal has shown modest recent flashes (7.8 ppg). Bust: real college scoring pedigree that a back surgery and thin opportunity have kept from NBA production.

name: Jaime Jaquez Jr.
notes: UCLA's Pac-12 Player of the Year and Lute Olson Award winner as a senior (17.8/8.2, a four-year, 1,802-point career), elite winning production and feel from a proven college star. Miami took him 18th, the only Pac-12 first-rounder that year. Jaquez delivered immediately (11.9 ppg, All-Rookie First Team, 4th in Rookie of the Year voting), was benched for stretches in 2024-25, then broke out as a genuine sixth man in 2025-26 (15.4 ppg, NBA-leading bench points, runner-up Sixth Man of the Year) before a 2026 blockbuster trade to Milwaukee (the Giannis deal). Hit: real, winning college production that became a genuine, high-value NBA role player.

name: Brandin Podziemski
notes: An Illinois-to-Santa Clara transfer who broke out immediately as WCC co-Player of the Year (19.9/8.8/3.7, 43.8% from three, Wisconsin Mr. Basketball in high school), elite all-around guard production from a mid-major after a buried freshman year. Golden State took him 19th. Podziemski delivered instantly (All-Rookie First Team, 9.2/5.8/3.7) and grew every season (11.7, then a career-high 13.8/5.1/3.7 across all 82 games in 2025-26). Hit: a massively undervalued transfer breakout that became a genuine, ascending NBA starter.

name: Cam Whitmore
notes: A five-star Villanova one-and-done (12.5/5.3, Big East Freshman of the Year) whose pre-draft buzz reached top-five range before a fall to 20th on off-court makeup questions, real elite scoring efficiency (leading the NBA in points per touch as a rookie). Houston took him 20th. Whitmore's role shrank as Tari Eason returned (12.3 to 9.4 ppg) before a 2025 trade to Washington was followed by a serious deep vein thrombosis diagnosis that ended his season; a further 2026 trade to Cleveland led to a waiver. Bust relative to his top-five pre-draft buzz, his career now complicated by both role uncertainty and a significant health scare.

name: Noah Clowney
notes: A four-star Alabama freshman (9.8/7.9/0.9 blk on 48.6% FG), real stretch-four rebounding upside on a thin one-year sample. Brooklyn took him 21st. Clowney needed two patient years (5.8, then 9.1 ppg, an ankle injury cutting 2024-25 short) before a real 2025-26 breakout — a full starting role, career highs including a 31-point/seven-three game, 12.3/4.1 across 66 games (60 starts). Hit: real developmental upside that matured into a genuine NBA starter.

name: Dariq Whitehead
notes: A consensus five-star Duke recruit and Naismith Prep Player of the Year (8.3/2.4/1.0 on efficient 40.8/41.1% shooting), elite recruiting pedigree undercut by injury even in his lone college season. Brooklyn took him 22nd. Whitehead's NBA chance stayed almost entirely in the G League across two Nets seasons (1.5 to 5.7 ppg in limited action), a 2025 waiver, and a brief but promising 10-day Memphis stint (a career-high 16.3 ppg, a 26-point game) in 2026. Bust relative to his recruiting hype, though real recent flashes of NBA-level scoring.

name: Kris Murray
notes: Iowa's First-Team All-Big Ten and Third-Team All-American junior breakout (20.2/7.9/2.0), real go-to scoring production, the twin brother of 2022 lottery pick Keegan Murray. Portland took him 23rd. Murray settled into modest Blazers rotation minutes (6.1, dipping to 4.2, then a 5.8 ppg uptick), before a June 2026 blockbuster trade (part of the Ja Morant deal) sent him to Memphis. Bust relative to his college scoring volume, though a real, sustained NBA rotation role has held.

name: Olivier-Maxence Prosper
notes: A Clemson-to-Marquette transfer whose production spiked as a junior (12.5/4.7/0.9 stl), real athletic forward upside from a four-star recruit. Sacramento took him 24th (traded to Dallas with Richaun Holmes). Prosper's early Mavericks role stayed marginal (3.0, then 3.9 ppg) before wrist ligament surgery ended his 2024-25 season and led to a waiver; a 2025 Memphis two-way deal produced real growth (a 25-point game) and a standard contract in March 2026. Solid outcome: real athletic tools that steadily developed into a genuine NBA roster spot after injury and a fresh start.

name: Marcus Sasser
notes: Houston's consensus First-Team All-American and Jerry West Award winner as a senior (16.8 ppg, AAC Player of the Year, a toe injury that cut short a 17.7 ppg junior year), elite winning-program scoring pedigree. Memphis took him 25th (traded to Detroit in a three-team deal). Sasser's role and efficiency shrank every season with the Pistons (8.3 to 6.6 to 5.2 ppg) before a 2026 six-team trade sent him to Dallas. Bust: elite college scoring production that never scaled into a real, expanding NBA role.

name: Ben Sheppard
notes: A four-year Belmont riser who closed his college career as First-Team All-Missouri Valley (18.8 ppg as a senior, after 16.2 ppg as a junior), real, proven mid-major scoring development. Indiana took him 26th. Sheppard has grown every NBA season (4.4 to 5.3 to 7.1 ppg, expanding minutes and starts each year) into a genuine, established Pacers rotation player with real playoff experience (38 games across two runs). Solid outcome: steady, patient four-year college development translating into steady, patient NBA development.

name: Nick Smith Jr.
notes: A consensus five-star, 247Sports No. 1 overall 2022 recruit whose lone Arkansas season was limited to 17 games by a persistent knee injury (12.5 ppg), elite recruiting pedigree on a health-limited, incomplete sample. Charlotte took him 27th. Smith's rookie shooting was historic (43.2% from three at 19 or younger, matching only Jayson Tatum) and he grew into more of a role (9.9/2.4/2.1 in 2024-25) before a 2025 waiver and a Lakers two-way deal that converted to a standard contract, including real 2026 playoff minutes. Solid outcome: elite shooting talent finding a genuine NBA role after an injury-limited college evaluation.

name: Brice Sensabaugh
notes: Ohio State's Big Ten All-Freshman honoree (16.3/5.4 on 48.0% FG), real go-to scoring instincts on a one-year sample. Utah took him 28th. Sensabaugh developed steadily every season (7.5 to 10.9 to a career-high 14.9 ppg in 2025-26 on markedly improved 46.0/42.2% shooting), highlighted by a 43-point game that included a record 21 bench points in a single first quarter. Hit: real scoring instincts that matured into a genuine, high-volume NBA scorer.

name: Julian Strawther
notes: A three-year Gonzaga developmental riser who broke out as a First-Team All-WCC junior (15.2/6.2/1.3, a 35-foot buzzer-beater against UCLA), real shot-making growth from a winning program. Indiana took him 29th (traded to Denver). Strawther's role expanded steadily (4.5 to 9.0 to 7.2 ppg with more starts), including a real 2025 playoff contribution (15 points in the final 14 minutes of a Game 6 elimination game). Solid outcome: patient college development translating into a genuine, growing NBA rotation role.

name: Kobe Brown
notes: A four-year Missouri senior and First-Team All-SEC honoree (15.8/6.4, SEC Scholar-Athlete of the Year), real all-around production from a proven college veteran. LA Clippers took him 30th. Brown spent three quiet seasons as Clippers depth (2.0 ppg as a rookie, heavy G League time) before a February 2026 trade to Indiana (part of the Bennedict Mathurin deal) unlocked real opportunity — 9.4/4.9/2.0 across 27 games including 10 starts, earning a two-way re-signing. Mixed outcome: real college production that needed a change of scenery to find a genuine NBA role.

name: James Nnaji
notes: An 18-year-old EuroLeague big man (ESPN's No. 24 prospect) who developed through Barcelona's academy since 2019, a genuine draft-and-stash project with modest actual production (2.2 ppg in EuroLeague, 4.3 ppg in a Liga ACB title season). Detroit took him 31st, his rights traded twice (Charlotte, then New York as part of the Karl-Anthony Towns deal). Nnaji never signed, instead parting ways with Barcelona in 2025 and unexpectedly enrolling in U.S. college basketball — Baylor, then George Mason by mid-2026. Never played in the NBA — an unusual path from EuroLeague prospect back to college ball.

name: Jalen Pickett
notes: A Siena-to-Penn State riser and consensus Second-Team All-American senior (15.6/5.6, a 41-point game, 2,000 career points, Penn State's first 40-point scorer since 1961), elite winning production from an older, four-year prospect. Indiana took him 32nd (traded to Denver). Pickett needed patient development (1.6, then 4.1 ppg) before a real 2025-26 expanded role (5.2 ppg, 18 starts, a first career triple-double, a 29-point game) — Denver declined his fourth-year option in 2026, and he signed a two-way deal with the Clippers. Mixed outcome: real, patient development into a genuine NBA rotation piece, though not retained long-term.

name: Leonard Miller
notes: A Canadian prospect who grew from 6'4" to 6'10" in 18 months and skipped college for G League Ignite (15.1/8.6/1.6 on 50% FG, a top-2 recruit by On3), elite physical-development upside on a thin professional sample. San Antonio took him 33rd (traded to Minnesota). Miller's Wolves role stayed marginal for years (1.7, 1.5, then 2.3 ppg) before a February 2026 trade to Chicago (part of a deal involving Ayo Dosunmu and Julian Phillips) fully unlocked him — 11.7/5.8/1.3 across 27 starts. Hit: real, elite physical upside that patient development and a change of scenery finally converted into genuine NBA production.

name: Colby Jones
notes: Xavier's Second-Team All-Big East junior and NIT MVP (15.0 ppg on 50.9% FG, leading Xavier to the 2022 NIT title), real all-around wing production from a winning program. Charlotte took him 34th (traded to Sacramento). Jones's NBA chance stayed marginal in Sacramento (2.1, then 1.1 ppg) before a 2025 trade to Washington produced his best NBA stretch (8.7/4.3/2.5 across 15 games) — a further 2025 trade to Oklahoma City led to an immediate waiver, a one-game Detroit stint, and a brief, medically-ended Spanish league signing. Bust: real college winning production that thin NBA opportunity across four organizations never let sustain.

name: Julian Phillips
notes: A consensus five-star, top-20 recruit whose lone Tennessee season showed real tournament-stage scoring (8.3/4.7, a team-leading 13.3 ppg at the Battle 4 Atlantis). Boston took him 35th (traded to Chicago via Washington). Phillips developed gradually with the Bulls (2.2 to a career-best 4.6 ppg) before a February 2026 trade to Minnesota (part of the Ayo Dosunmu deal) produced real minutes, including five playoff games, and a July 2026 free-agent signing with Houston. Mixed outcome: real recruiting-era talent that has found modest, genuine NBA roster spots across three organizations.

name: Andre Jackson Jr.
notes: UConn's junior team captain and starter on the 2023 national title team (6.0/5.8 career, a title-game start with six assists), elite defensive versatility and winning pedigree from a champion. Orlando took him 36th (traded to Milwaukee). Jackson carved out a real, sustained defensive-wing role with the Bucks (2.2 to 3.4 ppg, 43 starts in 2024-25) and won the 2024 NBA Cup, before a reduced 2025-26 role led to an August 2026 Exhibit 10 signing with Toronto. Solid outcome: real defensive versatility that held a genuine multi-year NBA rotation role and a title.

name: Hunter Tyson
notes: A five-year Clemson senior (using a COVID extra year) and First-Team All-ACC honoree in his final season (15.3/9.6, the Skip Prosser scholar-athlete award), real, late-blooming production from an older prospect. Oklahoma City took him 37th (traded to Denver). Tyson's NBA role stayed marginal across three Nuggets seasons (2.2 ppg, never more than 7.8 minutes) before a 2026 trade to Brooklyn and immediate waiver sent him to Puerto Rico's Gigantes de Carolina, where he's thrived (18.0/5.9 as a starter). Bust: real, late-college production that a crowded Denver roster never let translate into consistent NBA minutes.

name: Jordan Walsh
notes: A consensus five-star, top-25 recruit and Arkansas Sweet 16 freshman (7.1/3.9/1.1 stl, rated the class's best two-way player by ESPN), real defensive-wing upside on modest offensive production. Sacramento took him 38th (traded to Boston for the rights to Colby Jones). Walsh won a championship as a rookie in a bench role, then needed two quiet development years (1.7, then 1.6 ppg, heavy G League time) before a real 2025-26 breakout — 5.4/4.0 across 25 starts — earning a $2.4M team option pickup. Hit: patient multi-year development into a genuine, ascending NBA rotation player and champion.

name: Mouhamed Gueye
notes: Washington State's First-Team All-Pac-12 sophomore breakout (14.3/8.4, a 31-point game against USC), real shot-blocking and rebounding upside on a two-year sample. Charlotte took him 39th (traded to Atlanta). A stress fracture wiped out most of his rookie season (6 games), but Gueye developed into a real Hawks rotation piece — a 28-start 2024-25 (6.0/4.2, an 18-rebound game) and further growth to 4.9/3.8 across a 77-game 2025-26 (a career-high 21-point game) — before a fractured foot required 2026 surgery. Mixed outcome: real defensive-big development interrupted repeatedly by injury.

name: Maxwell Lewis
notes: Pepperdine's Second-Team All-WCC sophomore breakout (16.6 ppg, real shot-creating tools scouts liked), a season-ending wrist injury having cost him development time as a freshman. Denver took him 40th (traded to the Lakers). Lewis won the inaugural NBA Cup as a rookie but barely played (0.3 ppg), and a 2024 trade to Brooklyn was followed almost immediately by a fractured tibia; waived in mid-2025, his career has since continued through Turkey's Tofaş, Lithuania's Juventus Utena (a 13.6 ppg LKL Finals run) and, by 2026, a loan from Žalgiris Kaunas to London Lions. Bust: real shot-creation tools that injuries and thin opportunity never let develop into consistent NBA minutes.

name: Amari Bailey
notes: A five-star UCLA freshman and California Mr. Basketball (11.2/3.8/2.2, a strong 49.5/38.9% Sweet 16 shooting stretch), real guard scoring and shot-making upside on a thin freshman sample. Charlotte took him 41st. Bailey's NBA chance stayed minimal (2.3 ppg over 10 games) before a 2024 Brooklyn waiver and two-plus G League seasons (Long Island, Iowa); by 2026 his career shifted to Israel's Hapoel Jerusalem. Bust: real recruiting-era guard talent that thin NBA opportunity never let develop past two-way and G League depth.

name: Tristan Vukcevic
notes: A 7'0" Partizan Belgrade power forward who impressed at the 2023 Combine (21 points in 17 minutes), real stretch-big scoring and athleticism upside. Washington took him 42nd. Vukčević signed in 2024 and developed into a steady, real rotation contributor immediately — 8.5, then 9.4, then 9.0 ppg across three seasons on strong 43-50% shooting — earning a three-year, $9M standard contract in 2026. Hit: real stretch-big scoring translated directly into a genuine, sustained NBA role.

name: Rayan Rupert
notes: A French wing who developed through INSEP and Centre Fédéral before a New Zealand Breakers Next Stars season, real long-term two-way upside on a young, unrefined sample. Portland took him 43rd. Rupert needed three patient, G League-heavy Blazers seasons (3.3/1.8 career) before a February 2026 waiver and a Memphis 10-day signing unlocked a real breakout — a 33-point/10-10 triple-double against Milwaukee, career highs of 12.2/6.4/2.1 across 16 games — before a July 2026 Philadelphia signing. Hit: patient long-term development that finally produced a genuine NBA breakout after a change of scenery.

name: Sidy Cissoko
notes: A Baskonia academy product and the first European to sign with G League Ignite, elite international pedigree (ESPN's third-ranked European prospect in the class) on thin direct production. San Antonio took him 44th. Cissoko's early NBA chance stayed marginal (3.8 ppg with the Spurs) before 2024-25 trades through Sacramento and Washington led to a Portland two-way signing that finally stuck — a real 2025-26 rotation role (5.1/2.2 across 75 games) and 2026 playoff minutes. Solid outcome: real international development that took several organizations to find a genuine NBA rotation spot.

name: GG Jackson II
notes: A consensus five-star, the top-rated recruit in his class, whose lone South Carolina freshman season showed real go-to scoring on inefficient shooting (15.4/5.9 on 38.4% FG, SEC All-Freshman). Memphis took him 45th, a notable draft-slide given his recruiting rank. Jackson broke out fast after Grizzlies injuries opened a path — a 44-point/12-rebound game made him the youngest player ever with a 40-10 game, All-Rookie Second Team honors (14.6 ppg) — before a broken foot requiring surgery limited 2024-25 (7.2 ppg); he bounced back to 12.5 ppg in 2025-26. Hit: real elite scoring talent that, once given an opportunity, became a genuine young NBA scorer.

name: Seth Lundy
notes: A four-year Penn State riser (14.2/6.3 as a senior, honorable mention All-Big Ten, the first Penn State duo drafted alongside Jalen Pickett), real, patient college development. Atlanta took him 46th. Lundy's NBA chance stayed minimal and turbulent — ankle surgery in 2024, a Hawks waiver, a brief Clippers two-way stint before a 2025 release — leaving him a free agent. Bust: real four-year college production and shooting that never found a lasting NBA opportunity.

name: Mojave King
notes: A New Zealand NBL Next Stars product (Cairns Taipans, then G League Ignite) who bypassed NCAA offers, real long-term athletic wing upside from a non-college path, becoming just the third New Zealand-born draftee ever. LA Lakers took him 47th (traded to Indiana). King never earned real NBA minutes, spending his time in Indiana's G League affiliate (3.9 ppg) before his rights traded twice more (New Orleans, Houston) without a signing; by 2026 he plays in Greece's Mykonos and has earned New Zealand national team call-ups. Bust: real athletic upside that never crossed over from G League depth to NBA opportunity.

name: Jordan Miller
notes: A George Mason-to-Miami riser who capped his career with a rare perfect-shooting Elite Eight performance (7-for-7 FG, 13-for-13 FT, matching Christian Laettner) after a Second-Team All-ACC fifth-year senior season (15.3 ppg), real winning, efficient production from an older, well-traveled college path. LA Clippers took him 48th. Miller needed two quiet development years (1.6, then 4.1 ppg) before a real 2025-26 breakout (10.0/3.0/2.3 across 60 games), earning a three-year, $15.3M extension in 2026. Hit: patient, multi-year development into a genuine, well-paid NBA rotation player.

name: Emoni Bates
notes: Once the most hyped high school recruit of his generation, whose stock crashed after an injury-limited, disappointing Memphis freshman year (9.7/3.3 on 38.6% FG) before a genuine Eastern Michigan bounce-back (19.2/5.8, a 29-straight-point half against Toledo). Cleveland took him 49th, a stunning fall from his once-generational billing. Bates's NBA chance never developed (2.7, then 3.7 ppg on two-way deals) through arthroscopic knee surgery in 2024, and by late 2025 he was waived by Philadelphia and traded to the G League's Texas Legends. Bust: the steepest recruiting-hype-to-outcome collapse in the class, injuries and inefficiency compounding at every level.

name: Keyontae Johnson
notes: A First-Team All-SEC Florida sophomore (14.0/7.1) whose career was upended on December 12, 2020, when he collapsed on the court and spent three days in a medically induced coma; after transferring to Kansas State he returned to full form as Big 12 Newcomer of the Year and First-Team All-Big 12 (17.4/6.8, an Elite Eight run), a genuine comeback story. Oklahoma City took him 50th. Johnson's NBA chance stayed minimal (1.2 ppg over 9 games) before a 2024 Charlotte waiver and G League time; by 2026 his career has continued in China's CBA with Shandong Hi-Speed Kirin. Bust at the NBA level, though a real, inspiring return to competitive basketball after a life-threatening on-court collapse.

name: Trayce Jackson-Davis
notes: Four-year Indiana big who broke out as a redshirt junior (20.9/10.8/4.0 ast/2.9 blk) on the strength of elite rim protection, quick-twitch leaping, and unusually good passing feel for a center. Pre-draft evaluators flagged one clear cap on the profile: essentially no shooting range outside 15 feet, which pushed a first-round-caliber defensive/passing skillset all the way to 57th overall. The NBA arc has tracked that scouting almost exactly — Jackson-Davis carved out real rotation value with Golden State as a lob-catching, rim-running backup five with legitimate defensive playmaking, but the offensive ceiling never opened up. By year three his minutes eroded (36 G, 4.2/2.7 with GSW) and he was dealt to Toronto at the deadline (17 G, 3.4/2.7). Solid outcome: a genuine NBA rotation piece, capped exactly where the pre-draft report said he'd be capped.
